Pyoderma gangrenosum — sterile neutrophilic dermatosis (matches full epidermal necrosis, dense neutrophil-rich dermal infiltrate and focal fibrinoid vessel necrosis; nonresponsive to antibiotics; culture/PCR negative). Consider systemic immunosuppression (high‑dose corticosteroids or cyclosporine) and avoid surgical debridement; dermatology referral for management.

2. Fixed drug eruption — classic for solitary genital lesions and can show epidermal necrosis with eosinophils; patient has multiple prior drug exposures. Review drug timeline, stop suspected culprit; consider patch testing and clinic follow-up.

3. Behçet disease — genital ulcers often neutrophilic with vascular involvement; consider if there is history of recurrent oral ulcers, ocular inflammation or pathergy. Recommend targeted history/exam (oral ulcers, eye symptoms) and rheumatology/DERM evaluation.

4. Cutaneous small‑vessel vasculitis / necrotizing vasculitis — focal fibrinoid necrosis of superficial vessels and polymorphonuclear infiltration compatible with leukocytoclastic/vasculitic process; evaluate for systemic vasculitis (ANCA, CBC, ESR/CRP, urinalysis, complement).

5. Atypical infection or malignancy (herpes simplex, atypical mycobacteria, deep fungal infection, or squamous cell carcinoma) — less likely given negative stains/cultures and PCRs so far but cannot be fully excluded. Recommend targeted confirmatory tests if clinical suspicion persists (HSV PCR from lesion swab, repeat/deeper biopsy with immunostains and HPV/SCC evaluation).

Rationale summary: sterile neutrophil‑predominant necrosis with negative microbiology and poor antibiotic response favors a neutrophilic/immune-mediated cause (pyoderma gangrenosum most likely); other possibilities include drug reaction, Behçet, vasculitis or an occult infection/malignancy that may require focused testing.
